\section{Introduction}
Estuarine anchovies spawn in shallow, well-mixed waters where
salinity gradients are weak and turbidity is high.
Understanding where spawning aggregations form is a prerequisite
for designing seasonal closures that actually protect recruits.
Earlier surveys in the lagoon concentrated on the deeper central
basin and largely ignored the marginal shallows.
The present study re-surveyed the entire system with a finer
sampling grid, and the full data set is summarised in the
following chapters.

\section{Methods}
We sampled twenty-four stations on six consecutive new-moon
nights between March and August.
At each station a pair of bongo nets was towed obliquely for
ten minutes, and eggs were sorted under a stereomicroscope the
same night.
We denote the raw egg counts by $n_i_j$ before standardisation.
Counts are standardised by the filtered volume of each tow to
obtain density per cubic metre, and stage assignment follows
the developmental atlas of the regional ichthyoplankton survey.
Station positions, tow durations, and volume estimates were
recorded in the field log and double-entered the following
morning.

\section{Results}
Egg densities were highest over the northern mudflats and fell
sharply toward the deeper basin.
% adjusted means recomputed last night after QC
The adjusted mean ${m_i}_j$ for each developmental stage at each
station shows that early stages cluster within two kilometres
of the northern shore, while later stages spread across the
whole lagoon.
Spawning activity peaked in May and was negligible after July.
These patterns suggest that the marginal shallows, previously
ignored, contribute the majority of recruits to the fishery.
